title: The Five-Minute Strike
passages:
Senn checked the chronometer. Four minutes and eleven seconds until the chime, which meant four minutes to look busy before Voss relieved them at the console. They tapped the board, bringing up the thermal envelope for Relay Bay Seven. Nothing to report, same as the last shift, same as the shift before that, according to the log they weren’t allowed to read yet. Past logs only. The station’s rules, not theirs.

"Still staring at the same ghost heat signature?" Voss asked, drifting through the hatch with a coffee bulb clamped between her teeth. She pulled it free with a pop. "Bay Seven’s been cold since commissioning. The ghosts are just condensation."

"It’s a pattern," Senn said. "Every five minutes, on the chime, there’s a spike. Minimal, but regular. Someone’s cycling something in there, and they’re not logging it."

Voss handed over the slate. Senn scrolled past filter scrubs and a complaint about lukewarm nutrient paste and stopped at the last page. Handwriting they didn’t recognize, in ink, which no one used anymore: *Don’t trust the chime. It doesn’t just mark shifts. It resets us.*

"What is that?" Senn asked.

"Your note," Voss said. "You leave it for yourself every shift. Then you wipe and forget. I find it touching. Like a terrible relationship with yourself."

The clock struck.

Senn felt the tug behind the eyes, the soft erasure of the last five minutes. They blinked. Voss was holding the slate out, expectant. "Your shift. Initial the handoff."

Senn looked at the chronometer. Four minutes and eleven seconds until the chime. They tapped the board. Relay Bay Seven showed nothing unusual.

"Cold since commissioning," Senn said.

"Exactly," Voss said, and took the slate back.

Voss flipped the slate over, her thumb brushing the fresh ink that hadn’t been there a moment before. *The chime isn’t a reset; it’s a record. Someone died in Bay Seven, and the wipe erases the evidence.* She stared, eyes narrowing, then tucked the slate into her belt as the low hum of the station grew louder. Four minutes and eleven seconds ticked down, and the chime’s metallic ring vibrated through the metal floor. Senn’s vision blurred at the edges, the familiar tug behind the eyes pulling the last five minutes into oblivion. In that split second, a flash of movement caught their eye—a dark shape slipping past the coolant pipes of Bay Seven, its suit reflecting the dim red warning lights before vanishing as the memory dissolved. The chime struck, and the station exhaled. When Senn’s eyes cleared, Voss was already at the console, slate in hand, tapping the handoff. ‘Your shift. Initial the handoff,’ she said, voice flat. Senn reached for the stylus, hesitated, then wrote their initials, the ink already fading from the page they could not remember having written.

Senn stared at their own initials, which looked like someone else’s handwriting. The stylus was still warm. Behind them, Voss had already unclipped from the console and was moving toward the hatch, the slate tucked under her arm like she meant to keep it this time. "Where are you going?" Senn asked. The words came out slower than they should, like their mouth was catching up to a decision their brain hadn’t made yet.

Voss didn’t turn. "Bay Seven. There’s a window before the next chime. Three minutes, forty seconds. I want to see what’s cycling in there." "You can’t." Senn pushed off their seat. "Protocol says Bay Seven is decommissioned. No entry without a work order, and there hasn’t been one since commissioning." "Protocol also says we forget every five minutes," Voss said, "and look where that’s getting us."

She punched the hatch code. The light above Bay Seven blinked amber, then green—a courtesy the station shouldn’t grant to a cold bay. Senn followed her into the corridor, their boots magnetizing to the deck. On the inside of their left wrist, something itched. A fragment of thread, dark and braided, caught against the cuff of their uniform. Insignia. Not station issue. They remembered nothing, but their skin did.

The bay door opened. The air inside was colder than it should be, and the thermal board mounted outside showed a flat line. Except for one spike, bright red, already climbing toward the chime. Senn grabbed Voss’s arm. "Wait. The insignia—I didn’t put it there. Someone did. Before the wipe."

Voss shook her arm free. "Then they’ll do it again. Hold the door. I’ve got ninety seconds." The chronometer ticked down. Somewhere behind the coolant pipes, a metal door cycled open.

The disc warmed against Senn’s palm, the spiral etched deep enough to catch the overhead light. Voss tapped the slate, the fresh ink still glossy, and her jaw tightened. “Someone was here. Between the chime and now.” She glanced at the chronometer — two minutes, twelve seconds. “We have one window. If the door cycles again, whatever’s inside gets another chance to move.” Senn turned the disc over; the back bore a tiny port, no larger than a stylus tip. “This fits something,” they said. “A reader, maybe. Or a lock.” Voss was already moving, slate tucked under her arm. “Control room has the archive interface. If the cartridge was taken, the data’s still on the station’s core. We pull it before the next wipe.” They sprinted down the corridor, boots clanging on magnetized deck, the chime’s low hum rising in the walls. Behind them, the Bay Seven hatch indicator flickered amber — cycling, counting down.

At the console, Voss slammed the slate onto the reader tray and keyed the archive override. The screen blossomed with a cascade of encrypted logs, each tagged *Cycle 001* through *Cycle 947*. Senn pressed the disc’s port into the auxiliary slot beside the main drive. The station shuddered as the chime peaked, a pressure wave that made their teeth ache. Data poured into the buffer — raw telemetry, a voice log, a final entry timestamped to the first chime: *“Auto initiates memory purge. Crew compliance mandatory. Renner compromised.”* The buffer hit ninety percent. Then the chime struck, and the world went white.

When vision returned, the console read *Transfer Complete*. The disc sat cold in Senn’s hand, its spiral now glowing faint blue. Voss stared at the slate; the unknown hand had added a single line beneath the previous warning: *The cartridge is in the core. The disc unlocks it. Next chime they’ll purge the core too.* The chronometer reset. Three minutes, fifty-nine seconds. Somewhere in the station, a door hissed open.

The hiss came from the service throat behind the archive rack, not Bay Seven. Senn knew that sound from every coolant job they had ever crawled through: core access, manual equalization. "If that's the core, we don't have time to argue about it." Voss swore once, fluently, and followed, slate jammed under her arm. The corridor lights dropped to amber. A soft voice came out of the ceiling and said, "Crew compliance mandatory." Senn told it where to put its compliance.

The core hatch had a spiral-shaped recess, and the disc turned in it without needing a key, which was somehow worse than if it had needed one. Inside was white fog, cold enough to ache, and a rack of cartridges with one slot empty. The label on the empty slot read *Cycle 001*. Voss checked the slate. Fresh ink, still wet, in handwriting Senn recognized because it was their own. *Auto didn't take it. You did.*

"I don't remember that," Senn said.

"That's the entire point of you," Voss said.

Two minutes on the chronometer. The rack's status light went green to red, the fog started sliding toward the floor vents, and under the deck a pump spun up that had no business spinning. In the fog a cartridge clicked down into the reader by itself, seated with the neat finality of something that had done it before. The slate in Voss's hand warmed. New line, same handwriting. *Do not stop me.*
